lines.content: Scoutly is adapted from [AddressBook Level 3 by SE-EDU](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3). It uses [JavaFX](https://openjfx.io/) for the desktop interface, [Jackson](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson) for JSON persistence, [JUnit 5](https://junit.org/junit5/) for tests, and [MarkBind](https://markbind.org/) for this website.
* @sidharthbairy used OpenAI Codex to generate and refine implementation code and regression tests for hiring-stage features and bug fixes.
* Codex was used for preliminary PR reviews, checking correctness, SE-EDU coding standards, duplicated code, and the Single Level of Abstraction Principle (SLAP).
* Codex assisted with exploratory testing, reproducing bugs, diagnosing their causes, and suggesting fixes.
* Codex helped draft and refine documentation, PlantUML diagrams, GitHub issue reports, and PR descriptions.
* [@antaradaw](https://github.com/antaradaw) used OpenAI Codex extensively across their Scoutly contributions
to generate and refine implementation code, write tests, investigate and fix bugs, and draft and revise
project documentation, including work on candidate profiles and follow-up reminders.
Refer to the guide [_Setting up and getting started_](SettingUp.md).
The ***Architecture Diagram*** given above explains the high-level design of the App.
The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)
<puml src="diagrams/UiClassDiagram.puml" alt="Structure of the UI Component"/>

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`. All of these, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.
`Logic#getAllPersons` exposes the address book's read-only observable source list. `PipelineDashboard`
observes that list for global hiring-stage totals, and observes `getFilteredPersonList` separately for
the displayed count. `PipelineSummary` computes immutable counts for all five stages.
`ViewCommand` resolves its target through the existing index/name lookup and returns it in
`CommandResult#getProfileTarget`. `MainWindow` uses this structured target to open the profile; it does
not parse feedback text. `CandidateSelectionModel` tracks immutable replacements using source-list
replacement positions, including name/phone edits. After each command, the window reconciles visibility
and restores the list highlight. User list gestures update profile selection; automatic selection
changes during deletion do not select a different profile. A failed command restores the prior profile
when the rolled-back candidate remains visible, including failed delete and clear operations.
The list displays the model's filtered and sorted order directly, keeping command indexes consistent
with `list sort/name`, stage filters and follow-up filters. Follow-up reminders appear on compact
cards and in the full profile, including completion state and notes. Profiles display only stored current stages;
there is no stage-history or job-role data in the model.
Bulk stage updates snapshot the selected `Person` targets and send one `stage INDEX[,INDEX]... s/STAGE`
command. `StageCommand` resolves every displayed index against a snapshot before modifying any candidate,
so a stage filter cannot remove an earlier row and retarget a later selection. Invalid stages, empty
selections, duplicate indexes, and out-of-range indexes are rejected before any candidate is changed.
The central `workspaceScroll` contains the dashboard, toolbar and candidate/profile split pane. Header
placeholders use their preferred heights, while a minimum split-pane height keeps profiles usable.
When the window or command suggestions leave less room, the central viewport scrolls instead of
shrinking header containers below their content. Bulk and profile action rows use wrapping flow panes.
Command entry, feedback and the status bar stay outside the scrolling area. Layout regression tests
check section bounds and scrolling at default and minimum window sizes, with suggestions open.
`CommandHistory` maintains a bounded session history and an independent unfinished draft.
`CommandSuggestionProvider` computes token-range replacements without invoking command execution.
`CommandSuggestion` preserves input outside that range, including arguments after the caret.
`CommandBox` retains invalid input and routes every submitted command through its existing executor.
`CommandAssistPanel` handles suggestion presentation and contextual syntax.
`CommandReference` is the shared immutable catalogue for suggestions, syntax help, and searchable
`HelpWindow` entries. It reuses command `MESSAGE_USAGE` constants where available. Templates are
inserted through a callback; only Enter executes them. Feedback uses an error pseudo-class alongside
explicit Success/Error text. JavaFX focus changes preserve the input's anchor and caret.
JavaFX regression tests share `FxTestUtil` so the toolkit starts once per test worker. `MainWindowTest`
exercises real command execution, save rollback, and layout integration, and writes a rendered workspace

Candidate cards display the hiring stage as a labelled badge. `PersonCard` derives a stage-specific CSS class from the `HiringStage` enum name using `Locale.ROOT`. `PersonListCard.fxml` keeps the badge at its content width, while `Workspace.css` defines its colours. The stage name remains visible so that users do not need to distinguish stages by colour alone. When a candidate is updated, `PersonListPanel` rebuilds the affected card with its current stage.
`PersonCardTest` loads the current workspace theme and checks that all five stage backgrounds are distinct, with text contrast of at least 4.5:1 in both normal and selected cards.

`ViewCommand` delegates candidate matching to the shared `PersonLookup` helper.

It passes that candidate object to `Model#deletePerson`, rather than passing the index. An out-of-range

Before execution, `EditCommandParser` tokenizes and validates every `s/` value. An empty or invalid skill
raises a `ParseException` before a command is constructed, without changing the model or saving data.
`EditCommand` validates the displayed index, selects the candidate, and replaces the complete skill set
while preserving all other fields, including the hiring stage and follow-up. An invalid displayed index
raises a `CommandException` without changing the model. A successful edit shows all candidates in stored
order and returns a `CommandResult`. `LogicManager` saves only if candidate data changed; a failed save
restores the original data, filter, and comparator before reporting an error, as described under the

1. When `Logic` is called upon to execute a command, the command is passed to an `AddressBookParser` object, which in turn creates a parser that matches the command (e.g., `DeleteCommandParser`) and uses it to parse the command.
1. This results in a `Command` object (more precisely, an object of one of its subclasses e.g., `DeleteCommand`) which is executed by the `LogicManager`.
1. The command can communicate with the `Model` when it is executed (e.g. to retrieve the displayed list and delete a person).
1. The result of the command execution is encapsulated as a `CommandResult` object which is returned from `Logic`.
Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.
* stores the address book data i.e., all `Person` objects (which are contained in a `UniquePersonList` object).

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)

**Note:** The alternative, arguably more object-oriented, design below keeps a unique list of tags in `AddressBook`, and each `Person` references tags from that list. This lets `AddressBook` maintain one `Tag` object per unique tag instead of each `Person` holding its own `Tag` objects.
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)

JSON loading requires exactly one root value; trailing whitespace is allowed, but additional values or malformed trailing content cause a loading error. Invalid candidate files abort startup and remain unchanged. `JsonUserPrefsStorage` also rejects null GUI settings before model initialization, so invalid preferences produce a warning and are replaced with defaults through the existing recovery path. Missing GUI settings retain their default values.

`MainApp.init` acquires a `DataFolderLock` before reading or writing candidate data or preferences. The lock uses `FileChannel.tryLock()` on `data/scoutly.lock` and remains held until shutdown. A competing instance skips initialization, displays a message, and exits without touching either JSON file. Initialization failure releases the lock immediately; shutdown releases it even if saving preferences fails. Process termination also releases the operating system lock. The lock file is retained, so its existence alone does not indicate that the folder is in use.

`DataFolderLock` resolves the real data-folder path and tracks active locks within the JVM. This prevents aliases from opening a second channel for an owned lock file: on some systems, closing any channel for that file can release the process's locks. The operating system lock additionally protects against separate JVMs.

`LogicManager` compares its pre-command `AddressBook` snapshot with the resulting data. It saves only when they differ. Read-only commands, changes to the displayed filter or sorting, and unchanged candidate updates therefore do not rewrite the file. Failed saves of changed data still restore the original candidate data, filter, and comparator.

JSON saves write the complete UTF-8 content to a temporary file in the destination directory, then atomically replace the saved file. A failed write or replacement preserves the previous file and removes the temporary file. If the filesystem does not support atomic replacement, saving reports an error instead of falling back to an unsafe overwrite. Existing POSIX file permissions are preserved, and read-only destinations are rejected.
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.

`ViewCommand` resolves full names using `PersonLookup.findByName`. For ambiguous names, its callback formats only the matching candidates with their one-based indices in the current displayed list, names, and phone numbers. Phone numbers distinguish candidates even when optional email fields are empty. The command leaves candidate data and the displayed list unchanged, so the user can select a match with `view INDEX` immediately.
`view INDEX` selects a candidate by position in the currently displayed list. `view FULL_NAME` instead
uses `PersonLookup` to match normalized full names, ignoring case, within that same list.
The following sequence diagram focuses on `ViewCommand.execute` and the three full-name lookup outcomes.
Command parsing, individual profile getters, feedback formatting, and result-object creation are omitted.
<puml src="diagrams/ViewProfileSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Full-name candidate profile lookup, including missing and ambiguous matches" />
A missing or ambiguous name raises a `CommandException`. For an ambiguous name, the message lists the
matching candidates' displayed indices, names, and phone numbers, with guidance to use `view INDEX`.
A unique match produces a `CommandResult` containing formatted profile feedback and the candidate as
a structured profile target via `CommandResult.showProfile`. The UI opens that candidate's profile
without parsing the feedback text. The command leaves candidate data, the active filter, and displayed
order unchanged, so displayed indices remain suitable for a subsequent command.

Each `Person` stores a non-null `HiringStage` enum: `APPLIED`, `SCREENED`, `INTERVIEW`, `OFFERED`, or `REJECTED`. Constructors without an explicit stage default to `APPLIED`. Stage changes affect full person equality, while identity continues to depend on the normalized name and phone number.

`AddressBookParser` routes `stage INDEX s/STAGE` to `StageCommandParser`. The parser uses `ArgumentTokenizer` with `PREFIX_STAGE` (`s/`), validates the positive displayed index, rejects repeated stage prefixes, and parses a case-insensitive stage name. Missing arguments or a missing prefix and invalid indices produce usage errors; empty or unknown stages produce a list of allowed values.

`StageCommand` resolves the candidate using the current filtered list. If the requested stage is already current, it returns `[Name] is already at [Stage].` without replacing the candidate. Otherwise, it replaces that candidate with a new immutable `Person` through `Model#setPerson`. It preserves every other field and the current filter. All transitions, including backwards moves and setting the current stage again, are allowed so recruiters can correct mistakes. `EditCommand` and `RemarkCommand` carry forward the existing stage when replacing a person.

`PersonCard` displays a stage badge, and `ViewCommand` includes it in structured profile output. `JsonAdaptedPerson` persists the stage name in the `stage` JSON field. Missing or null stages in older data default to Applied; unrecognized or blank stored stages are rejected with an `IllegalValueException`. Existing fixtures without stages exercise backward compatibility, alongside new valid-stage and invalid-stage fixtures.
`SummaryCommandParser` accepts `summary` without arguments; `AddressBookParser` routes it to `SummaryCommand`. Extra parameters are rejected with command usage instructions.

`SummaryCommand` reads `Model#getAddressBook().getPersonList()` so the summary includes all candidates, independently of the active filter. It counts stages in an `EnumMap` in one pass and formats every `HiringStage` in enum order, using zero for absent stages, followed by the total. Counts are recalculated on every invocation. The command does not replace candidates or modify the displayed list, filter, or order.
### Deleting a candidate by full name
`delete FULL_NAME` searches only the currently displayed candidates. `DeleteCommand` delegates the lookup
to the shared `PersonLookup` helper, which normalizes whitespace and compares entire names ignoring case.
A candidate hidden by the current filter cannot be selected by name.
The following sequence diagram focuses on `DeleteCommand.execute` after a full name has been parsed.
It keeps the unique, missing, and ambiguous lookup outcomes. Command parsing, ambiguity-message
formatting callbacks, result-object construction, and persistence are omitted.
<puml src="diagrams/DeleteByNameSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Full-name deletion with unique, missing and ambiguous candidate matches" />
A missing name raises a `CommandException`. For multiple matches, `PersonLookup` invokes the ambiguity-message
callback supplied by `DeleteCommand`. The message includes each match's actual displayed index, stored name,
and phone number, and asks the user to choose with `delete INDEX`. Neither error path deletes a candidate or changes
Only a unique match reaches `Model#deletePerson`, passing the resolved `Person`. The command returns a
`CommandResult` identifying the deleted candidate. Hidden candidates remain stored, and the active filter
and relative order of the remaining candidates are preserved. After successful command execution,
`LogicManager` saves the updated data; a failed save restores the original data, filter, and comparator
before reporting an error, as described under the [Storage component](#storage-component).

`AddCommandParser` accepts one name, one phone number, and one or more skills. It rejects unknown prefixes and repeated name or phone fields. `Name` normalizes whitespace, requires a leading letter or number, and limits newly entered names to 100 characters. `Phone` accepts 7–15 digits with an optional leading `+`. `Skill` accepts 1–30 alphanumeric characters without spaces. Duplicate skills are removed case-insensitively, preserving the first spelling.

Candidate identity is the normalized, case-insensitive name together with the exact phone number. Matching only one field does not make a duplicate. New candidates have stage Applied and empty optional contact details, tags, and remark. `EditCommandParser` accepts skill replacements alongside contact fields. `EditCommand` preserves fields not supplied, including stage and remark. A supplied skill set replaces the previous set; a bare `s/` is rejected.

`find` matches full words in candidate names using OR semantics. `findskill` supports a complete single-skill match and `any` or `all` prefixed skill queries. Skill matching is case-insensitive. `list s/STAGE` uses a stage predicate. All these commands expose results through the same displayed list, so subsequent indexed commands act on those results.

`ModelManager` wraps the stored candidates in a `FilteredList` and then a `SortedList`. `list sort/name` applies a case-insensitive name comparator without changing stored order. Updating the filter clears this comparator. Plain `list` therefore shows all candidates in stored order; sorting is a display operation and is not persisted. `view`, `summary`, and successful deletion preserve the active display order and filter. Adding, editing, or updating a remark shows all candidates in stored order.

`RemarkCommandParser` accepts a displayed index and at most one `r/` field. Omitting the field or supplying an empty value removes the remark. Repeated prefixes produce a parse error before the model or storage is changed. `RemarkCommand` replaces the selected immutable `Person`, preserving every other field, and resets the displayed list to all candidates. Notes are persisted in the JSON `remark` field.

`MainApp` reads preferences and `data/addressbook.json` relative to the launch directory. A missing candidate file initializes sample data. Invalid or unreadable candidate data aborts startup with an explanatory error, preserving the original file. These cases must be tested separately. Missing or unreadable preferences use defaults instead.

`LogicManager` parses and executes a command, then saves the candidate data through `StorageManager` only when the candidate data changes. Before execution it snapshots the data, active predicate, and comparator. If saving throws an `IOException`, it restores those values and reports the storage error. `JsonAdaptedPerson` supports legacy names and phone numbers already stored under the earlier constraints; this compatibility does not relax validation for newly entered names or phone numbers.
Undo, redo, and data archiving are not implemented. Deletion and clearing are permanent unless the user restores a backup.
* recruits candidates and tracks their progress through a hiring pipeline
* prefers typed commands with a desktop list and profile display
* needs to search candidates by name or skill and review hiring-stage totals
* works with candidate data saved locally and available offline

**Value proposition**: Scoutly helps recruiters record candidate details and skills, maintain recruitment notes, and track Applied, Screened, Interview, Offered, and Rejected stages using typed commands and automatic local saving.

1. Scoutly must run on Windows, Linux, and macOS with the Java version specified by the project setup, currently Java `25` or above.
2. Scoutly must respond to normal commands within 2 seconds for a contact list containing up to 1000 contacts on a supported computer.
3. Scoutly must save contact changes automatically after every successful command that changes data.
4. Scoutly must store contact data in a local JSON text file that a technically proficient user can read and edit.
5. Scoutly must preserve all valid contacts when saving and loading the local data file, and must report invalid data instead of silently treating it as valid.

6. Scoutly must support one local user at a time and must not require a network connection for normal contact management. At most one instance may use a given data folder at a time; separate home folders may be used independently.
7. A user who is comfortable typing regular English text must be able to complete the common add, edit, find, list, and delete tasks using commands without relying on mouse navigation.
8. Invalid commands, invalid candidate fields, duplicate candidates, and invalid indexes must produce a clear user visible error without changing the existing valid candidate data.
9. Scoutly must be distributable and launchable as a JAR without requiring a project specific installer.
10. Scoutly must provide the same command behavior through its documented CLI on every supported operating system.
* **Address**: The postal or location information stored as one field of a candidate.
* **Command**: A keyword and its arguments entered by the user to request one operation from Scoutly.
* **Candidate**: A recruitment record containing a name, phone number, skills, hiring stage, and optional email, address, remark, and tags.
* **Displayed index**: The positive number shown beside a candidate in the current displayed list and used by commands such as `edit` and `delete`.
* **Email**: The electronic mail address stored in a candidate record.
* **GUI**: The graphical user interface that displays candidates and command results.
* **JSON data file**: The local text file used by Scoutly to persist candidate data between launches.
* **Mainstream OS**: A commonly used desktop operating system such as Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS.
* **Name keyword**: A word supplied to `find` for matching against candidate names without regard to letter case.
* **Parameter**: A value supplied to a command, such as an index, field value, or name keyword.
* **Phone**: The telephone number stored in a candidate record.
* **Tag**: An optional label attached to a candidate for grouping or identification.
`FollowUp` is an immutable value object stored on `Person`. It contains an optional
calendar date, a note of at most 200 characters and a completion flag. The empty state
cannot contain a note or be completed. Date validation requires an exact `YYYY-MM-DD`
format, a real calendar date and a year from 1 to 9999. Past dates are permitted.
and `followup INDEX clear`. Duplicate prefixes and mixed operations are rejected.
`FollowUpCommand` resolves the index against the displayed list, replaces the candidate
with `Person.withFollowUp`, and then restores the full list. Completing an absent or
already completed follow-up fails without changing data. Rescheduling replaces the note
and resets completion. Candidate edits and remark updates preserve the follow-up.
`FollowUpsCommandParser` parses an optional view, defaulting to pending.
`FollowUpFilter` supplies predicates for pending, overdue, today, upcoming, completed
and all follow-ups. Each predicate captures the command's local reference date so that
every candidate is evaluated against the same day. Listing always searches the entire
address book, retains its order and reports counts for the resulting view.
`JsonAdaptedFollowUp` validates stored fields before constructing the model object.
`JsonAdaptedPerson` defaults missing or null follow-up data to the empty state so older
files load successfully. A present follow-up object with missing fields, an invalid
date, an invalid note or inconsistent state is rejected. `PersonCard` displays the
date, status and note, and removes the label from layout when no follow-up exists.
Tests cover calendar boundaries, note validation, lifecycle transitions, filtered
indices, failed commands without mutations, all six views, preservation during other
edits, JSON round trips, older files, malformed stored objects and the JavaFX card label.
Run `./gradlew test checkstyleMain checkstyleTest` to verify the feature.

Scoutly is a **desktop application for managing recruitment candidates through typed commands**, with a graphical interface for viewing your candidate pipeline. You can store candidate details and skills, add recruitment notes, and track hiring stages from application to decision.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Open the latest [Scoutly release](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3/tp/releases), expand **Assets**, and download the `.jar` file for your computer.
Choose `scoutly-mac-arm64.jar` for an Apple Silicon Mac (M-series chip), or `scoutly.jar` for
an Intel Mac, Windows, or Linux. On Mac, check **Apple menu → About This Mac** to identify your chip.
1. Copy the file to a writable folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for Scoutly.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar scoutly.jar`.
**Apple Silicon Mac:** Run `java -jar scoutly-mac-arm64.jar` using an ARM64 Java 25 installation.
Launch Scoutly from a folder where you have permission to create and update files. If double-clicking the JAR does not work, use the terminal command above.
The application window should appear in a few seconds. On first launch, it contains sample candidates.
Use the command box to enter commands, the result area to read feedback, and the candidate list to find displayed indexes.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 s/Java s/SQL` : Adds a candidate named `John Doe` with two skills.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd candidate shown in the current list.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
The five dashboard tiles count **all stored candidates** by their current hiring stage, even during
a search. The displayed count shows how many candidates are in the current results. The tiles
update after additions, edits, stage changes, and deletions. They show current stages, not a history
Candidate cards show their current command index, stage, and up to three skills. Open the profile
for the complete skill list, contact information and follow-up details. An empty pipeline and a search with no matches
have different prompts; use `list` to reset a search.
The workspace toolbar provides quick controls for common browsing tasks:
* Type in **Find** to search candidates by name or skill. Select a hiring stage to combine
the stage filter with the text search, or choose **Clear** to restore the full list.
* Enable **Due follow-ups** to show pending follow-ups scheduled for today or an earlier date. Enable
**Needs contact** to find candidates whose email or phone number is missing; these smart filters can be
combined with the text and stage filters.
* Click a dashboard stage tile to activate that stage filter. Use **Refresh** to reapply the current in-memory
workspace filters; it does not reload candidate data changed externally in the JSON file.
* Use **Export CSV** or **Export JSON** to save the currently displayed candidates in their visible order.
The export includes contact details, address, hiring stage, skills, tags, remarks, and follow-up details.
* Select several candidate cards with Command-click (macOS) or Ctrl-click (Windows/Linux). **Stage selected**
applies one hiring stage to all selected candidates, while **Delete selected** asks for confirmation before
deleting them. Stage updates continue to target the selected candidates when a stage filter removes
updated rows. **Clear selection** removes the multi-selection.
* In a candidate profile, **Edit**, **Update stage**, **Add remark**, and **Delete** open the corresponding
command or confirmation without requiring you to retype the candidate index.
* Enable **High contrast** when stronger borders and text contrast are needed. The setting applies to the
current window and does not alter saved candidate data.
Toolbar filters remain active after candidate updates, including `followup`, `edit`, and `remark`.
They take precedence over those commands' list resets: only candidates matching all active toolbar
filters remain visible. An updated candidate can disappear if they no longer match a filter;
their saved data is retained. Recheck displayed indexes before the next command.
For example, with Alice and Ben stored and all other toolbar filters cleared, type `Alice` in the
toolbar's **Find** field, then run `followup 1 d/2026-11-05 r/Call`. Alice's follow-up is saved,
and only Alice remains visible because the toolbar search is still active. Click the toolbar's
**Clear** button or run `list` to show both candidates again.
Successful `list`, `find`, `findskill`, and `followups` commands clear the toolbar controls and display
their own results. For example, `list` restores all candidates, while `followups` shows pending
follow-ups. Changing a toolbar filter afterward replaces the command's results with the toolbar's
filters applied to all stored candidates.
On smaller windows, scroll the central workspace to reach the candidate list and profile. The dashboard
and toolbar retain their content height, action buttons wrap to fit the available width, and command
input and feedback remain visible outside the scrolling area.
| Up / Down | Recall older/newer commands when suggestions are hidden. Returning past the newest entry restores your unfinished draft. |
| Up / Down with suggestions open | Select a completion. |
| Ctrl+Up / Ctrl+Down | Recall history even while suggestions are visible. |
| Tab | Accept the selected command-name or hiring-stage completion. Existing arguments are preserved. |
| Escape | Dismiss suggestions until the input changes. |
| Ctrl+L (Windows/Linux), Command+L (Mac) | Focus the command box while preserving its text and caret. |
| F1 | Open or restore the offline command reference. |
Syntax help appears below the input for recognized command names. Suggestions do not execute commands;
press **Enter** to submit. Failed commands remain available for correction. History stores up to
200 attempted commands for the current session, omits consecutive duplicates, and resets when Scoutly closes.
Success and failure feedback use both text labels and different colours.

Only one Scoutly instance can use a home folder at a time. If you launch another instance from the same folder, it shows `Scoutly is already running with this data folder. Please use the existing window.` and closes after you dismiss the message. Use the window that is already open.
Before upgrading, close any windows opened by older versions of Scoutly.

Closing Scoutly releases the folder for the next launch. If Scoutly is forcibly terminated, the operating system releases the lock automatically; no manual cleanup is needed. Instances using separate home folders can run independently.
1. Add a candidate: `add n/Jordan Lee p/91234567 s/Java s/SQL`.
1. Run `list` to show all candidates and note Jordan Lee's displayed index.
1. Run `view INDEX`, replacing `INDEX` with that number, to inspect the candidate's profile.
1. Run `remark INDEX r/Available for interviews next week` to record a recruitment note.
1. Run `stage INDEX s/Interview` to update the hiring stage.
Use the candidate's current displayed index each time. Commands such as `find` change the displayed list,
so the same candidate may have a different index afterward. If the example candidate already exists,
use their displayed index or add a candidate with a different name or phone number.
Click a command to jump to its syntax, examples, and detailed explanation.
[`list`](#listing-candidates-list) | Show all candidates, filter by stage, or sort by name.
[`summary`](#summarizing-the-hiring-pipeline-summary) | Count candidates at each hiring stage.
[`remark`](#adding-or-removing-a-remark-remark) | Add, replace, or remove a recruitment note.
[`delete`](#deleting-candidates-delete) | Delete candidates by displayed index or full name.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `remark INDEX [r/REMARK]` can be used as `remark 1 r/Available immediately` or as `remark 1`.
* Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/shortlisted` or `t/shortlisted t/referral`.
* Command words are case-sensitive. Separate the command and prefixed fields with ordinary spaces.
* Parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* Leading and trailing spaces around values after prefixes such as `n/`, `p/`, and `s/` are ignored.
For example, `add n/  Alice  p/  91234567  s/  Java` is equivalent to `add n/Alice p/91234567 s/Java`.
* Extraneous parameters for `help`, `exit`, and `clear` are ignored.

For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. The `list` command accepts either the optional `s/STAGE` or `sort/name` parameter, but not both, and the `summary` command rejects extra parameters; use it on its own.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
Opens a searchable, offline command reference. Search by command name, description, or syntax,
then select a command to read its usage and examples. **Insert template** places a starter command
in the command box for you to complete. It never executes the command automatically.
You can also open the reference with **F1** or **Help → Command reference**.
Opening help again restores it if it was minimized.
You can also open the [Scoutly user guide](https://AY2627S1-CS2103T-T09-3.github.io/tp/UserGuide.html) directly.
Adds a candidate to the pipeline. New candidates start in the **Applied** hiring stage and have empty email,
Use `stage INDEX s/STAGE` after adding a candidate to change its hiring stage.
* At least one `s/SKILL` is required. Multiple skills may be provided.
* Names must contain 1–100 characters and start with a letter or number. Remaining characters may be letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, or apostrophes. Leading/trailing whitespace is
removed and repeated spaces are normalized.
* Phone numbers must contain 7–15 digits and may have one leading `+`.
* Skills must contain 1–30 alphanumeric characters with no spaces.
* Duplicate skills are removed case-insensitively, preserving the first spelling.
* A candidate is a duplicate when both the normalized name (ignoring case) and phone number match. Candidates with
the same name but different phone numbers, or different names but the same phone number, are allowed.
Successful additions use the message `New candidate added: NAME | PHONE | Skills: SKILL1, SKILL2`.
* Invalid names report `Invalid name: names must start with a letter or number, may only contain letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes, and must be 1-100 characters long.`
* Invalid phone numbers report `Invalid phone number: must be 7-15 digits, optionally starting with +.`
* Invalid skills report `Invalid skill: skills must be 1-30 alphanumeric characters with no spaces.`
* Missing skills report `At least one skill (s/) must be provided.`
Duplicate candidates report `This candidate already exists in your pipeline (same name and phone number).`

Shows candidates currently stored in Scoutly and reports the number of candidates listed. You can optionally filter the list by hiring stage. If there are no candidates, Scoutly displays `No candidates in your pipeline yet. Use 'add' to add one.`
* `STAGE` must be **Applied**, **Screened**, **Interview**, **Offered**, or **Rejected**. Stage names are case-insensitive.
* `list s/Interview` displays only candidates currently at the Interview stage.
* If no candidates match the selected stage, Scoutly displays `No candidates found at the Interview stage.`
* Invalid parameters show either the command usage instructions or the allowed stage values.
Use `list sort/name` to display candidates in ascending alphabetical order by name. Name sorting is case-insensitive.

The plain `list` command restores the stored candidate order, which follows insertion order; it clears any active search, stage filter, or alphabetical sort. Displayed indexes can change. Recheck the candidate’s index before viewing, editing, or deleting.
The only supported sorting parameter is `sort/name`; sorting cannot be combined with a hiring-stage filter. Use either
* `list` displays all candidates in stored order.
* `list sort/name` displays all candidates alphabetically by name.
Shows the number of candidates at every hiring stage and the total number of stored candidates.
* Always counts **all stored candidates**, including candidates hidden by `find` or another filter.
* Shows Applied, Screened, Interview, Offered, and Rejected in that order, including stages with zero candidates.
* Leaves candidate data, displayed order, and the current filter unchanged.
* Recalculates the counts each time, reflecting additions, deletions, and stage changes.
* Takes no parameters; extra arguments show usage instructions.
* The summary appears in the command result area. Scroll within that area to read the full result.
An empty pipeline shows zero for every stage and the total. Running `summary` after `find Jordan` still summarizes the entire pipeline while keeping Jordan's search results visible.
Opens the candidate's name, phone, email, address, tags, remark, current hiring stage, and skills
in the **Candidate profile** panel. Scroll within the panel to read long profiles. Tags and skills
are shown in alphabetical order. Missing tags or skills appear as `None`; empty email, address,
or remark fields appear as `Not provided`. Copy buttons let you copy available contact details.
The profile also displays the scheduled follow-up date, status and note, or `No follow-up scheduled`.
You can also select a candidate in the list using the mouse or keyboard. The profile refreshes
after edits. Deleting the candidate or hiding them through a search clears the profile;
a failed save restores the previous profile and candidate data.
* `INDEX` must be a positive integer referring to the currently displayed list.
* Viewing a profile leaves the candidate data and the displayed list unchanged.
* A successful `view` selects only the candidate whose profile is opened, replacing any earlier bulk selection.
Use Command-click (macOS) or Ctrl-click (Windows/Linux) to select several candidates for bulk actions.
* `FULL_NAME` must match the full name of exactly one candidate in the displayed list, ignoring case.
Leading/trailing whitespace is removed and repeated internal whitespace is treated as one space,
* Name lookup follows the same rules as `delete FULL_NAME`. Partial names do not match.
* All-digit input is treated as an index. Use the displayed index to view a candidate whose full name is numeric.
* A missing or malformed argument shows the command usage. An index outside the displayed list shows an error.
* If no displayed candidate matches the name, Scoutly suggests using `list` to show all candidates.
* If multiple displayed candidates match the name, the error lists their displayed indices, names, and phone numbers. Use `view INDEX` with one of those indices to choose the intended candidate.
* `list` followed by `view 2` displays the second candidate's profile.
* `find Betsy` followed by `view 1` displays the first candidate in the search results.
* `view alice pauline` displays Alice Pauline's profile if she is in the displayed list.
Edits an existing candidate in your pipeline.
* Edits the candidate at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed candidate list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values. After a successful edit, candidates are displayed in stored order,
with any active toolbar filters reapplied. With no active toolbar filters, all candidates are displayed.
Recheck indexes before the next command.
* Editing candidate details or tags preserves the candidate's skills, remark, and hiring stage. Use `remark` or `stage` to change the remark or stage.

* If one or more `s/SKILL` fields are provided, they replace all existing skills. Skills must be 1–30 alphanumeric characters; duplicate skills are removed case-insensitively while preserving the first spelling. If no `s/` field is provided, existing skills are preserved.
* Successful edits use candidate-oriented feedback; when skills are changed, the resulting skills are listed in deterministic alphabetical order.
* Every `s/` prefix must be followed by a valid skill. A bare `s/` is rejected.
* When editing tags, all of the candidate's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a candidate's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
*  `edit 1 p/91234567 e/johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of the 1st candidate to be `91234567` and `johndoe@example.com` respectively.
*  `edit 2 n/Betsy Crower t/` Edits the name of the 2nd candidate to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing tags.
Finds candidates whose names contain any of the given keywords.
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `hans` matches `Hans`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Hans Bo` matches `Bo Hans`.
* Only full words match; for example, `Han` does not match `Hans`.
* Candidates matching at least one keyword are returned (an `OR` search); for example, `Hans Bo` returns `Hans Gruber` and `Bo Yang`.
* A successful search reports the number of matching candidates using candidate terminology.
* `find alex david` returns `Alex Yeoh` and `David Li` if those candidates are in your pipeline.
* A single-skill search is case-insensitive and matches the complete skill name; for example, `findskill java`
matches `Java`, but `findskill SQL` does not match `NoSQL`.
* `any` returns candidates with at least one of the specified skills.
* `all` returns candidates with every specified skill.
* The skill must contain 1–30 alphanumeric characters with no spaces.
* Skills supplied with `any` or `all` are deduplicated case-insensitively, preserving the first spelling.
* If no candidates match, Scoutly displays `No candidates found matching skill search: SKILL(S).`
* The displayed indexes are renumbered after filtering and can be used by subsequent commands.
* `findskill Java` returns candidates with the `Java` skill.
* `findskill any s/Java s/Python` returns candidates with Java or Python.
* `findskill all s/Java s/SQL` returns candidates with both Java and SQL.
Adds or replaces the remark for a candidate in the currently displayed list.
* `INDEX` must be a positive integer referring to the displayed list.
* Example: `remark 2 r/Available for interviews next week`.
* Use `remark 2 r/` (or `remark 2`) to remove the remark.
* Remarks are shown on candidate cards and saved with your candidates. Editing other details preserves the remark.
* After changing or removing an existing remark, all candidates are displayed again unless toolbar filters
are active. Active toolbar filters are reapplied; use the toolbar's **Clear** button or `list` to show all candidates.
* Setting the same remark again reports `Remark unchanged for NAME.` Removing an already-empty remark reports
`NAME has no remark to remove.` Both leave candidate data, the displayed list, and its sort order unchanged.
* Successful updates report `Added remark to candidate: ...` or `Removed remark from candidate: ...`.
Schedules one follow-up per candidate, with an optional note. The candidate card shows
the date, note and whether it is overdue, due today, upcoming or completed.
* `INDEX` refers to the currently displayed list and must be a positive integer.
* Dates must be valid calendar dates from `0001-01-01` to `9999-12-31`, using exactly `YYYY-MM-DD`.
* Past dates are accepted, allowing recruiters to record an overdue task.
* Notes are optional, limited to 200 characters, and cannot contain control characters or line breaks.
* `d/` and `r/` may appear in either order. Repeating either prefix is rejected.
* Scheduling again replaces the previous date and note, and marks the follow-up as pending.
Omitting `r/` clears the previous follow-up note. This note is separate from the candidate's remark.
* `followup INDEX done` marks the follow-up completed while keeping its date and note.
It fails if no follow-up exists or it is already completed.
* `followup INDEX clear` removes the follow-up, including its note and completion state.
* A successful update clears command-based searches and follow-up views, but reapplies any active toolbar
filters. With no active toolbar filters, all candidates are displayed again. To restore the full list,
click the toolbar's **Clear** button or run `list`. Editing candidate details or remarks preserves the follow-up.
* Follow-ups are saved with candidate data and restored on the next launch. Older data files remain supported.
`pending` | All unfinished follow-ups; this is the default when the view is omitted.
`all` | All candidates with a follow-up, including completed ones.
* Every view excludes candidates without a follow-up.
* Views search the entire candidate list, including candidates hidden by a previous `find`.
* View names are case-insensitive. Only one view may be supplied.
* Results retain the usual candidate order and display new indices for use with `followup`, `edit` and `delete`.
* The result message includes the number of matching candidates and counts overdue and due-today tasks within that view.
* Dates use your computer's local calendar day. Run the command again after midnight to refresh the view.
* These are in-app reminders; the application does not send notifications while closed.
* Use `list` to display all candidates again.
* `followups overdue` shows unfinished follow-ups whose dates have passed.
* `followups today` shows the candidates to contact today.
Sets the hiring stage of one or more candidates in the currently displayed list.
* `INDEX` must be a positive integer from the displayed list. After `find`, it refers to the search results.
Separate multiple indexes with commas, for example `stage 1,3,5 s/Interview`. All indexes are resolved
against the displayed list before any stage is changed, so the command remains correct even when an
active stage filter causes an updated candidate to disappear from the results.
* The `s/` prefix is required and may appear only once. `STAGE` must be **Applied**, **Screened**, **Interview**, **Offered**, or **Rejected**. Stage names are case-insensitive.

* Any stage can be changed to any other stage, including going back to correct an earlier update. Setting the same stage again is allowed and reports `[Name] is already at [Stage].` without changing the candidate.
* The command preserves the current search filter and all other candidate details.
* The stage appears on the candidate's card and in `view INDEX`, and is saved automatically across restarts.

* Candidate cards show a labelled stage badge: Applied in grey, Screened in blue, Interview in purple, Offered in green, and Rejected in red. The stage name is always shown, so you do not need to rely on colour. Badges reflect the current stage after an update.
* New candidates and older saved records without a stage default to **Applied**. Editing details or remarks preserves the stage.

* Missing arguments or an invalid index format show usage instructions. An empty or unknown stage shows the allowed values; an index outside the displayed list shows an error. Failed commands do not change the candidate's stage.
* `stage 1 s/Interview` moves the first displayed candidate to Interview.
* `stage 1,2 s/Interview` moves the first and second displayed candidates to Interview as one operation.
* Running it again for Alex Yeoh already at Interview displays `Alex Yeoh is already at Interview.`
* `find Betsy` followed by `stage 1 s/screened` moves the first search result to Screened, keeping the search results visible.
* `stage 1 s/Applied` resets that candidate's stage to Applied.
Permanently deletes one candidate by index or full name, or several candidates by their displayed indexes.

* All formats select candidates from the **currently displayed list**. After a `find` or `findskill` command, only candidates in its results can be deleted. Use `list` first to select from all candidates.
* `INDEX` refers to the index number shown in the displayed list and **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* For batch deletion, separate indexes with commas, for example `delete 1,3,5`. Spaces around commas are allowed,
and indexes may be supplied in any order.
* All indexes refer to the list **before the command runs**. For example, `delete 1,3` deletes the original first
and third candidates, even though the displayed indexes change after deletion.
* Every index is checked before deletion. Duplicate indexes, empty entries, non-integers, non-positive values,
values larger than 2147483647, or indexes outside the displayed list cause the entire command to fail:
**no candidates are deleted**. For example, `delete 1,1`, `delete 1,`, and `delete 1,999` (when fewer than 999
* Batch deletion accepts indexes only; do not mix names and indexes or use ranges such as `delete 1-3`.
Names containing spaces, including numeric names such as `1 3`, retain full-name lookup behavior; use commas
* Successful batch deletion reports the number of deleted candidates and their details in the order of the
supplied indexes. Candidates hidden by the current filter remain stored, and the remaining displayed
candidates retain their order and filter.
* `FULL_NAME` must match the candidate's entire name, **ignoring case**. Partial names do not match. Do not put quotation marks around the name.
* Leading/trailing whitespace is ignored and repeated internal whitespace is treated as one space,
* If no displayed candidate matches the name, no record is deleted and an error is shown.

* If multiple displayed candidates match the name, no record is deleted. The error lists each matching candidate's displayed index, name, and phone number. Use `delete INDEX` with one of those indexes to choose the intended candidate.
* Input containing only digits is always treated as an index. To delete a candidate whose name consists only of digits, use their displayed index.
* Deletion removes the record completely; it does not archive the candidate. There is no undo command. Back up your data before deleting records you may need later.
* Deleting one candidate reports `Deleted candidate: ...`; batch deletion reports the number of deleted candidates.
* `list` followed by `delete 2` deletes the 2nd candidate in the candidate pipeline.
* `find Betsy` followed by `delete 1` deletes the 1st candidate in the results of the `find` command.
* `delete 1,3,5` deletes the original 1st, 3rd, and 5th displayed candidates.
* `findskill Java` followed by `delete 3, 1` deletes the 3rd and 1st displayed Java candidates, provided at least
three matches are displayed. Other candidates are preserved.
* `delete Alice Pauline` deletes the candidate named Alice Pauline if exactly one displayed candidate matches.
* `delete alice pauline` matches the same full name, ignoring case.

Use delete INDEX to choose a candidate.

The numbers refer to positions in the currently displayed list, including after `find`; they are not a separate numbering of the matches. In this example, `delete 3` deletes the candidate with phone number `81234567`.
Clears all entries from the candidate pipeline.
This removes every candidate, including candidates hidden by the current filter. There is no undo command. Back up your data first if you may need it later.
The success message is `Candidate pipeline has been cleared!`.

Scoutly automatically saves candidate data after each successful command that changes it. You do not need to save manually. Commands that only display information, change the displayed list, or exit do not rewrite the candidate file. Setting an existing value again also leaves the file unchanged.
Scoutly saves candidate data in `data/addressbook.json`, relative to the folder from which you launch the application.
If you follow the quick-start instructions, this is `[JAR file location]/data/addressbook.json`.
Advanced users can edit this file while Scoutly is closed. Back up the file first.
If the data file cannot be loaded, Scoutly aborts startup to prevent overwriting it. The existing file remains unchanged.
Correct the invalid data or restore a valid backup before launching Scoutly again.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause Scoutly to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Install Scoutly on the other computer. Close Scoutly on both computers, then copy `data/addressbook.json`
from the old home folder into the new home folder's `data` folder. Back up any existing destination file before replacing it.
Launch Scoutly from the new home folder to load your candidates.
